difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: one concept (the conditional-independence assumption of naive Bayes) settled by a single counting step (one class prior plus one Bernoulli parameter per attribute per class), about a minute for a prepared student.
stem: Given a dataset with $K$ binary-valued attributes (where $K > 2$) for a two-class classification task, the number of parameters to be estimated for learning a naïve Bayes classifier is

solution.quick: Naive Bayes assumes the attributes are conditionally independent given the class, so it needs only the class prior $P(Y=1)$ (**1** parameter) and one Bernoulli parameter $P(X_j = 1 \mid Y = c)$ for each of the $K$ attributes in each of the 2 classes (**$2K$** parameters). Total $2K + 1$, option **(B)**.

steps.title: What a naive Bayes classifier has to learn
steps.body:
Let the class be $Y \in \{0, 1\}$ and the attributes be $X_1, \dots, X_K$, each taking the value 0 or 1. Naive Bayes predicts

$$
\hat{y} = \arg\max_{c \in \{0,1\}} \; P(Y = c) \prod_{j=1}^{K} P(X_j = x_j \mid Y = c).
$$

The product form comes from the **naive** assumption: given the class, the attributes are conditionally independent. So the model is fully specified by

1. the class prior $P(Y = c)$, and
2. for every class $c$ and every attribute $j$, the one-attribute distribution $P(X_j \mid Y = c)$.

A "parameter to be estimated" is a **free** number: a probability that is forced by the others (because a distribution sums to 1) is not counted.

steps.title: Count the class-prior parameters
steps.body:
There are two classes. Write $P(Y = 1) = \pi$. Then $P(Y = 0) = 1 - \pi$ is determined by $\pi$.

Class prior: **1** free parameter.

steps.title: Count the class-conditional parameters
steps.body:
Each $X_j$ is binary, so its distribution within class $c$ is a Bernoulli distribution with one number:

$$
\theta_{jc} = P(X_j = 1 \mid Y = c), \qquad P(X_j = 0 \mid Y = c) = 1 - \theta_{jc}.
$$

There is one such $\theta_{jc}$ for every pair (attribute $j$, class $c$):

$$
\underbrace{K}_{\text{attributes}} \times \underbrace{2}_{\text{classes}} = 2K \text{ free parameters}.
$$

In training, each is simply a relative frequency, e.g. $\hat{\theta}_{jc} = \dfrac{\#\{\text{class-}c \text{ examples with } X_j = 1\}}{\#\{\text{class-}c \text{ examples}\}}$.

steps.title: Add up and check against the options
steps.body:
$$
\text{total} = \underbrace{1}_{\text{prior}} + \underbrace{2K}_{\text{conditionals}} = 2K + 1.
$$

For example, with $K = 3$ the model needs $\pi$ and $\theta_{10}, \theta_{20}, \theta_{30}, \theta_{11}, \theta_{21}, \theta_{31}$, which is $7 = 2 \cdot 3 + 1$ parameters. The options evaluate as follows:

| $K$ | (A) $2^K + 1$ | (B) $2K + 1$ | (C) $2^{K+1} + 1$ | (D) $K^2 + 1$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 3 | 9 | **7** | 17 | 10 |
| 4 | 17 | **9** | 33 | 17 |
| 10 | 1025 | **21** | 2049 | 101 |

Only (B) matches the count for every $K$. At $K = 2$, options (A), (B) and (D) would all equal 5; the stated condition $K > 2$ keeps the options distinct.

steps.title: Contrast: what the count would be without the naive assumption
steps.body:
Without conditional independence, the classifier would need the full joint distribution of $(X_1, \dots, X_K)$ within each class. That distribution has $2^K$ outcomes, hence $2^K - 1$ free parameters per class, and the total becomes

$$
1 + 2\,(2^K - 1) = 2^{K+1} - 1.
$$

This grows exponentially in $K$ (for $K = 10$ it is 2047). The naive assumption cuts it to the linear count $2K + 1$ (21 for $K = 10$), which is exactly why naive Bayes can be trained from little data. Hence the answer is **(B)**.

solution.teaching:
**Naive Bayes in one line.** Bayes' theorem says $P(Y = c \mid \mathbf{x}) \propto P(Y = c)\,P(\mathbf{x} \mid Y = c)$. The hard part is the class-conditional distribution $P(\mathbf{x} \mid Y = c)$ of the whole attribute vector. Naive Bayes makes one simplifying assumption: **given the class, the attributes are independent**, so

$$
P(\mathbf{x} \mid Y = c) = \prod_{j=1}^{K} P(x_j \mid Y = c).
$$

Instead of one big joint distribution per class, you learn $K$ small one-attribute distributions per class.

**How to count parameters.** A distribution over $r$ possible values has $r - 1$ free parameters, because the probabilities must add up to 1. So:

- a class variable with $C$ classes contributes $C - 1$ parameters;
- an attribute with $r_j$ values contributes $r_j - 1$ parameters **per class**.

General formula for naive Bayes with discrete attributes:

$$
(C - 1) + C \sum_{j=1}^{K} (r_j - 1).
$$

Compare this with the model without the independence assumption, which needs $(C-1) + C\left(\prod_j r_j - 1\right)$ parameters: exponential in $K$ instead of linear. This reduction is the whole point of the "naive" assumption. It also explains why naive Bayes works reasonably well on small training sets: each parameter is a simple frequency estimated from all examples of one class.

**Back to this question.** Here $C = 2$ and every $r_j = 2$ (binary attributes), so the count is $(2 - 1) + 2 \cdot K \cdot (2 - 1) = 2K + 1$, which is option (B). The distractors $2^K + 1$ and $2^{K+1} + 1$ carry the exponential flavour of the full joint model, which is precisely what naive Bayes avoids.

optionAnalysis.label: A
optionAnalysis.explanation: $2^K$ is the number of possible attribute vectors, which belongs to modelling the **joint** distribution of the attributes, not to naive Bayes. The naive assumption makes the count linear in $K$. For $K = 3$ this option gives 9, but naive Bayes needs 7.

optionAnalysis.label: B
optionAnalysis.explanation: One free class-prior parameter $P(Y = 1)$ plus one Bernoulli parameter $P(X_j = 1 \mid Y = c)$ for each of the $K$ attributes in each of the 2 classes: $1 + 2K$. This matches the official key.

optionAnalysis.label: C
optionAnalysis.explanation: This is close to the count for a full (non-naive) Bayes classifier, which needs $2^K - 1$ parameters per class for the joint distribution of the attributes: $1 + 2(2^K - 1) = 2^{K+1} - 1$. Naive Bayes does not model that joint distribution. For $K = 3$ this option gives 17, not 7.

optionAnalysis.label: D
optionAnalysis.explanation: A $K^2$ term would arise from parameters for **pairs** of attributes (interactions or covariances). Naive Bayes assumes the attributes are conditionally independent given the class, so it has no pairwise terms. For $K = 3$ this option gives 10, not 7.

solution.shortcut: Free parameters of discrete naive Bayes $= (\text{classes} - 1) + \text{classes} \times \sum_j (\text{values of } X_j - 1)$. With 2 classes and binary attributes: $1 + 2 \cdot K \cdot 1 = 2K + 1$.
solution.commonTrap: Counting both $P(X_j = 1 \mid Y = c)$ and $P(X_j = 0 \mid Y = c)$ as separate parameters (giving $4K + 2$), forgetting the class prior (giving $2K$), or slipping into the exponential count of the full joint model ($2^K$-type answers). Only probabilities that are not fixed by the sum-to-one constraint are parameters.

answerVerification.method: Author solve (not blind) compared with official key
answerVerification.notes: Naive Bayes with a binary class and K binary attributes needs 1 free class-prior parameter P(Y=1) and one Bernoulli parameter P(X_j=1 | Y=c) per attribute per class (2K), so 2K + 1 in total. A Python check fits the parameters on random binary data for K = 3, 4, 5, 10 and counts 7, 9, 11, 21, which matches only option B each time (the full joint model would need 2^(K+1) - 1). This agrees with official key B.
